utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, we are back in Courtroom III, second time today. Could you kindly call this case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Usual advisory, unless I hear from the accused that there are problems, I take it there are none. Defence teams seem to be in full force. Prosecution. It's Mr. McCloskey and Ms. Soljan and the case manager. So I take it from what I have heard that you would like to address the Trial Chamber on the leftovers of yesterday's incident or issue. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, Mr. Ruez. I apologise to you on behalf of the Trial Chamber for having kept you waiting for more than one hour. The reasons are two. One is technical because I had a Status Conference earlier on which finished at 9.00 and usually we require about 30 minutes before the courtroom is made ready for the next case. And secondly, is the last half an hour or so we dedicated to discussing the issue that was raised yesterday towards the ends of your testimony. We have discussed it, we have debated it, we have not concluded it. And you will today be asked questions which are not however related to the US-government-provided aerial images. Those questions will be put to you at some later date when you will be required to return to The Hague. In the meantime, consultations are taking place between Prosecution and the US government and we'll come to that stage later on. But I just wanted to inform you what the situation is. And be prepared that you will need to come again. I thank you for your understanding, Mr. Ruez. Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, uses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We were speaking yesterday about a couple of topics. I am going to try and narrow some down, but I still have a couple of questions on your process, investigative process with respect to witnesses. I know you shared some of it with us but on a different issue. What was the procedure or guidelines as to when you would tape record a conversation with a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tape recording was a procedure used when the witness had a status of a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that under no circumstances would you tape record unless you advised the witness that he was indeed a suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, why were not tape recordings used to interview key witnesses, for example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I think you need to explain who you are referring to in particular, because key witness? Who would decide?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought he covered it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- is a key witness. We are talking of 1995, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the term I think key witnesses when you were initially commencing your investigation, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was referring to those we name the survivors and I have already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And so was I. That's why I referred to them key because I thought you did. Those witnesses in particular, let's -- the victims, did you ever tape record their conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not in the rules and procedures of this Tribunal to record witnesses who are victims. It's a rule that is designed for interviews of suspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What if anything would have prohibited you from tape recording those victim witnesses, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For sure, nothing, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to suspects, is it only Serb suspects that you tape recorded or any suspects regardless of their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the rules of procedures of this Tribunal make no ethnic differences to -- in respect of to who they apply to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I know what those rules are. I'm asking about your personal investigative procedures and guidelines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Continuing on that line with respect to the witnesses, the majority, if not all of them, were non-English speaking, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think none of them was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought a couple may have but okay that's fare. None of them. With respect to the victims that you interviewed, did they, sir, explain the process a little more so I can get a better understanding. Is it that you would have a discussion with them and that that discussion would be an answer/question session and then you would reduce it in writing or how did the process work? You're smiling. You must know where I'm going again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm not smiling because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I won't ask you, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a difference of methodology depending on from what country one comes from. Coming from France, my methodology was to listen to the "stories", in brackets stories, the testimonies, the declarations of the witnesses, and I was typing meanwhile these people were talking. The interference with their speech was basically designed only to keep the chronology of what they were saying, in order to ensure the dates. Once that statement was taken, even if there was another interview or follow-up of interview the next day, I didn't touch the statement any longer, though it was not signed yet by the person. When I observed that the American way of doing it was that investigators were rewriting the statement during the evening, and having it confirmed by the witness the next day. So indeed, in the terms of presentation, they certainly looked better.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Which would be more accurate and concise with the testimony or the declaration that witnesses would give you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both are. Both are because the description I make of the method used by my American colleagues doesn't touch the essence of what the witness has said. It just formats it in a better way to make it easier to read for those who will read it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if I can ask you a couple more questions on that. When would the witness be given that statement in the language in which he or she may understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was during -- after a read back done by the interpreter at the end of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So they would really be never -- they would never really be given a written statement back in their own language, they would just be given an oral summary or an oral reading of their statement that you or another investigator reduced to writing, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the rule in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Don't ask me. Ask those who wrote these rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what rule are you referring to? Is it in the Tribunal Rules or is it in the OTP rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the witness acknowledgement that was pre-written on the statements that these witnesses were providing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I see that every statement and there is many of them, but who made that pre-acknowledgement form? Did the Tribunal make it? Did the Prosecutor make it? Did you as the person in charge of the investigation make that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm not the one who wrote this rule. This is a rule of the Tribunal, of the methodology to be used by the investigators and followed by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you were still employed with the OTP in 2001, obviously, during the Krstic trial, up until towards the end, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the process I'm interested to know is that when a witness that's been called by the Prosecutor comes into court, are they given then the English version of their statement to review in order to prepare for their testimony, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, don't ask me. This is not a part related to the investigation process. We are now entering the trial phase and I leave the hand to my colleague, the Prosecutor, to answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. That's clear. But let's turn no another topic if we may. I'd like to focus your attention on the period of July 12th through the 18th approximately 1995. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, when you investigated this case, did you confirm or corroborate with witnesses whether there was water, food and medical treatment in Potocari at that time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a water tank that we can see on the video that was shown during this testimony. We also know that UNHCR convoy arrived but arrived after all the refugees have left, had left, and aside the distribution of candies and cigarettes to the kids in Potocari, we have no knowledge of whatever assistance provided to the crowd of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, this UNHCR convoy that came, that came when, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it arrived the 13, and nothing was distributed that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, with whom did you discuss that nothing was distributed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a contact, I don't remember exactly how that was done, precisely, because it's a tiny detail in the investigation, but we had a contact with a name -- a man named Andre who was the leader of that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was this just a water that the UNHCR was bringing in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what was inside the convoy. No, I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever ask Andre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how we got -- honestly, I don't know how we got that information. But we know a witness talked about receiving any thing that came from that UNHCR convoy. The people were exiting the area at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May we, with the Court's permission, look at Exhibit ERN 00940583, with the court officer's permission?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would need a P or D number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 2D0002. Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We don't have ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking the question because on LiveNote, I have it, but on the main, we still don't have it. I just wanted to make sure that the witness can follow you. I mean, that we can follow you too. And the public. What's wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is this document that we are looking at which has the ERN number just for identification so that -- is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because earlier on, your assistant said 2D0002. But here I see 2D000010 and then it's the format which is different. So perhaps you can check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are going to check it but I think we can still proceed if I identify it adequately. I'm giving my learned colleague the ERN number so he can find it. There are two questions on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, we found it in another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you have the document in front of you, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, on the top right there is something written that's typed it in that says, just for identification purposes. It's not in exhibit in this case, but the way we received the document it has the letters OTPEX.113/1; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have it on the screen but you are certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And right underneath that, because it was probably used as an exhibit in another case, underneath that it has a set of numerical numbers which are 00940583. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't but it's surely on the document if you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know which exhibit Mr. Ruez is looking at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I'm getting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he's speaking of -- so we are on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It depends on what he says he has in front of him. And Madam Usher, could you kindly check? It's the same one, yeah. Okay so I'm assured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder if the accused is able to follow as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But they are in English. The document is in English anyway. So I doubt whether there -- is there B/C/S translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, as we go along, you're going to make specific reference to parts of it, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's restrict it to that. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, can you describe to us what that document is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You played a good description. It's obviously an AFP press release dated 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At -- where is it? 1926 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Going from the bottom, the fourth paragraph after the -- including the copyright material, do you see the paragraph which starts, "At 6.30 p.m., [1630 GMT]"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My focus is on that first sentence there. We can discuss the whole thing and we probably will with other witnesses but we are speaking here about food and water and medical treatment. We will get to that. It says here if I can read it and you agree or disagree "At 6.30 p.m., [1630 GMT], a six truck UNHCR convoy arrived at Potocari with water, food and news of the missing men." For my purposes, I'd like to stop here. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now is this the -- is this the same convoy you were referring to that you had a discussion with this UNHCR member Andre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no discussion with Andre, but this is exactly indeed the convoy I was referring to who arrived indeed at 6.30, so that's quite late in the afternoon of the 13. And we know from the UN troops in Potocari that by the end of the afternoon, let's say around 18, the entire deportation was over. So that's the reason why nothing of that convoy was delivered to the person it was designed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar, sir, with the fact that the United Nations had called this what you just identified quote "deportation" actually an evacuation? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of that. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did use also the word evacuation until the trial of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you this: If the UN calls it an evacuation and you call it something else, what's your basis for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The trial of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The judicial decision that was rendered by the Court, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, is there any doubt about the veracity of the statement here that's being reported that a six convoy UNHCR -- six truck convoy came to Potocari with both food and water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, this has not been part of the investigation. If it is written six, I have to trust the man who wrote it, but I have no idea if it was two or seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But those are my concerns with your investigation. First it's within the parameter that you set for the investigation, right, from the 11th to whatever the end date period was, let's say the 18th for our discussions here. This is the 13th. Wouldn't you as a prudent investigator who wants to give an objective and honest view to the Court, wouldn't you have investigated and verified that there was water, there is evidence of food, and try to find out if there is other instances or examples of food and water and medical treatment? Wouldn't you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fundamentally disagree with you on the way you present the situation. Due to the fact that this aspect was really a very, very tiny aspect in respect of all the other events that unfolded between the 12th and the 18th, as you put the frame, but I agree with you on the fact that everything has to be made in-depth and I forgot to tell you in my previous answer that this aspect was indeed dug into and that we also interviewed -- I interviewed both the mayor of Bratunac and I think the other one was the president of the opstina. Both of them had absolutely nothing to report about any event, bad event, that might have occurred in their town. But sad that they went -- I mean at least one of them, I think the mayor, went to Potocari with water and bread to be distributed to the 25.000 refugees. I mean the few bread he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you a little bit about the medical assistance that may have provided. What did your investigation find for the time period that we are discussing obviously, not 92 through 95 but only the time period that you discussed after the fall of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One aspect was more precisely investigated, but I must admit with little results, as far as I remember. It was the fate of the ones we called the sick and wounded. I think there were some 30 wounded who were moving back and forth apparently between Bratunac and Kladanj, and at one point we wanted to make sure of the fate of these people. I must admit that the result of that investigation inside the investigation was not really concluded. I would not be able yet -- and let's say that in the doubt, we have a knowledge that these people should be alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. It was my fault. I probably asked a poor question. Was medical assistance provided on or about July 13th, 1995, in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can see on the film, that is the one of Mr. Petrovic, that there is a medical tent in Potocari at a spot we named the blue house. This medical spot was apparently a UN Battalion medical tent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did your investigation at all find or determine that there was an UNPROFOR medical convoy of five to nine trucks providing transport and assistance to injured people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This was not something that jumped out of the events we were investigating.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But that would be significant, wouldn't it, if on July 13th, the day that you say most of the people left, despite that water and food was coming in, do you think that UNPROFOR would have sent five to nine vehicle transport to assist medically with injured people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is very possible, since UNPROFOR did not expect that the Serb forces had prearranged a large number of civilian vehicles to speed up the deportation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, if we can show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we will have a break in about four minutes time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I can get through this document in four minutes, I'm going to try.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The next exhibit, which is Exhibit number 2D0001, which is a -- [Microphone not activated] -- which is a nine page document. And if we could have the first page of the document on the ELMO -- on the screen, on the e-court screen, then we could just identify it and perhaps we could stop there. Mr. Ruez, if you could be kind enough to let me know when you get that first page and I'll proceed with my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So could you see on the top right-hand corner -- could you tell us what it stays? It seems to be a stamp of some kind, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a document coming from the UNHQ in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know that it's coming or going from there, but we can just read that stamp. I'll read it and you can tell me if I read it wrong. It says, "UNPROFOR communications" which is typed. There seems to be some handwriting either signature or date or something and underneath it has again typed form, "95 AUG-1 15:58". Could you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What's the top of that say, the caption actually of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a document that was sent by Keith Biazer [phoen] who was the UN head of office in Tuzla, to Peggy Hicks [phoen] which is an assistant of Keith Biazer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Isn't it -- not to interrupt you. Isn't it actually the other way around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was sent to him --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- from his assistant, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now just directing your attention quickly to page 5 of this document, if I may. It's actually page 7 of 9. Under Roman numeral subsection 4. I'm sorry, right above that, paragraph 23, do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph -- it's numbered 23.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm 11 to 15 on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. It would be the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 23, got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 23. Just that first sentence before the break quickly. Just -- I'll read it for you just so we make sure we are on the same page. It says, "An UNPROFOR medical convoy of between five and nine vehicles transporting 65-75 wounded and infirm people left Potocari on Wednesday, July 13, 1995." There is obviously more, but for our purposes I'm going to confine it to this sentence. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I'm reading the full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will just want to make sure we are on the same page, sorry. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, is, what if anything did you do to investigate further any of these medical convoys that UNPROFOR had which were transporting wounded and infirm people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not any of these convoys. It is that convoy. They were not dozens of convoys driving around in that area at that time. There was one. So indeed this is the information that we had, and that was later investigated specifically by one investigator of the team, but I told you about the results of this and as far as we know, these people are alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It may be a good time now. I do have another hour or so just to let the Court know approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, to continue on this line we are still looking at paragraph 23, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My question to you, during your thorough investigation, do you know if during the time period that we are discussing, again, just for the record and for your recollection, the 11th through the 18th of July 1995, was there any other medical evacuation of wounded and infirm people in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, your investigation, did you look into it at all? Did you ask anyone or did you ask UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had the accounts from the sit-reps and documents like the one you are showing. There was no additional investigation about that matter except for the event that is reported on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So just so I'm clear that I understand you, as far as you're aware, in your investigation, this was no other evacuation of wounded and infirm, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's look at one page before this document, paragraph 18. Are you with us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 18, it's the third line, second sentence. I'll read it if I may. If I may read that sentence -- again, we can go through the entire document, but for our limited purposes, I would just like to ask him this now if I may. On the third line it starts with the sentence, "While ICRC", do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes,.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just want to make sure we are on the same page. It says, "While ICRC was permitted to evacuate an additional 88 wounded or infirm persons from Bratunac and Potocari". Then it gives a date different from the date we just saw in paragraph 23 which was July 13 1995. What's the date that appears on paragraph 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 17, 18 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The same document that you said you reviewed and did your thorough investigation, tells us in one paragraph on July 13 there was a medical convoy evacuating people. Then you answer my question, sir, saying my investigation didn't find any. Other people being evacuated. And I'm directing your attention to paragraph 18. Isn't it true, sir, that your investigation, in fact, is not thorough and is not complete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say so, for the simple reason that I'm very happy for these 88 persons not to have ended up on the killing fields we know exist --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. If I may interrupt. I apologise. I usually don't interrupt. I'm not concerned with necessarily, and forgive me for saying this, your emotional state on this. My question is very straightforward. We have a document, the same document in two separate paragraphs. They talk about evacuating wounded and infirm people on two different dates, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to move on. What other evidence or what other investigative methods did you use to further examine if there were additional wounded or infirm people evacuated from Potocari in the period that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I don't really understand your point because if the document says that people are evacuated, so that means no crime has been committed against them. I'm investigating crimes; I'm not investigating evacuation of wounded from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you did no investigation, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this specific aspect, no, since the fate of these persons are written on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All I want to know, sir, is if you did an investigation based on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me intervene here. Mr. Ruez, you were tasked by the Office of the Prosecutor to carry out some investigations. Were you tasked to investigate every single alleged or suspected crime that was committed in or around Srebrenica during the relevant period or were you limited as to what you were supposed to investigate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The limitation only comes from the existing resources at that time. Had we had like it was the case in Belgium just before this investigation started, 300 police officers working on a rape case of children, we would certainly have investigated every murder, every physical abuse, or whatsoever. The fact is that in the course of this investigation, we had to focus on major crimes, the reason why I said at one point during my direct testimony, that during several years, on account of at least 30 people killed, we would not even move on the ground to check the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ostojic, you play proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I want -- thank you. I'm done with this document. I'd like to discuss you had mentioned in your direct examination basically a two-avenue approach for the people in Srebrenica, citizens of Srebrenica. One group, a civilian group, went towards Potocari, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the second group of individuals went in the -- in the military column went in the woods basically, or as you described it, up towards Tuzla, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just so that we understand each other. Now, the people, the civilians in Potocari, do you know how many there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The figure generally reported is around -- in Potocari? 25.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who uses this figure and how did you come up with it? Did you investigate to determine what the actual figure is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But you can imagine that these counts are always fuzzy. That count comes from various sources, mainly, I mean UN sources, DutchBat sources and I think there is even a report of that figure on a Bosnian Serb report, but I don't recall precisely that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In your investigation, sir, did you do or did you do any work to determine out of that civilian population how many were male?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been a very interesting thing to do but it was materially impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you did not do it, correct? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was done. But aside the faces that we can see on the Zoran Petrovic film, there is no way to have a proper account of how many men stayed in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, other than looking at the Zoran Petrovic film, what did you undertake as the lead investigator to determine what the population, civilian population in Potocari was? What was that male-women-children mix?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is -- these were UN sources mainly. Mainly the UNHCR who was providing the assistance in that area. And I know that the concern about this is that there is always a possibility of inflation of numbers in order to inflate humanitarian assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, didn't your investigation in fact confirm that that number, 25.000, approximately, is indeed within a reasonable margin of error accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, by crossing the various sources, I believe the number is approximately accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What are the sources that you crossed to determine that it was accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told you, UN sources, both HCR and DutchBat, as well as maybe the Prosecution might assist me on this, Bosnian Serb document that mentioned a figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are going to get to that document in a second. I'm sure you've seen it, but I'm just asking for your independent recollection now. Sir, out of those number of men in this group of 25.000 civilians, we know that they ended up where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you, sir, ever calculate to see how many of those 25.000 actually made it to the Tuzla area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That figure of 25.000 is the figure of those who arrived safely in Tuzla. We very well know that men were separated in Potocari so never made it to Tuzla. As well as at the arrival point at Kladanj and those also didn't make it to Tuzla, but again to know how many people are involved in this separation process, is an impossible task.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Are you familiar that in the Tuzla air base, that on or before July 19, 1995, 6.600 civilians from Potocari arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. I was on this base. This was the first spot where refugees were taken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well these refugees, did you take a count as to what that population was in terms of being male or female?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume UNHCR might have made such a count.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you didn't, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because we knew it was mainly women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know also that in the Tuzla town there were 500 such refugees who made it from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is only for talking about the town, yes, at the sports centre in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in Banovici, how many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, 3.500, does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several refugee centres around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about in Gracanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wait for you to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 1510. How about in Srebrenik, do you know how many were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're going to tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 3227. How about in Lukavic or Lukavac, 3617?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you go to all these individual villages and towns and places to look to determine how many male or female refugees, as you call them, who left Potocari and came to Tuzla? Did you get a count at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had no means to have any count of these refugees by independent sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It was a compound question. I apologise. Did you go to any of those towns to investigate any of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The witnesses we were interviewing during the summer 1995 were interviewed at the police station in Tuzla and they were picked up by a police officer and driven to the location where the interview took place. So we didn't move to these refugee camps. We had no time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a couple more towns that I'll mention or villages. As they are called. Zivinice. 3979?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, again I'm waiting for the final count now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will get to the final count. Kladanj, 500?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Dubovac, 1.500. Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, so fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So my count on this -- and if my arithmetic is correct -- and you may want to trust me on this is 24.933 is what the BiH government calculated based on these nine sites that we discussed or areas, if you will.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, so we are not far away from the assessment of 25.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Agree. When you talk about the inflation of numbers, isn't it true, Mr. Ruez, that really you're talking about the inflation of numbers for the military column and not the civilian refugees, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It is not correct. I was referring to a document that was -- I hardly remember. That was mentioning this possibility of inflation of numbers, but here we can see that at least for this one there is no inflation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may I have the witness be shown [Microphone not activated]. If I may, I'd like to have on the e-court and the witness to be shown 65 ter number 2D0003. And while they are getting it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I notice Mr. Lazarevic behind you. What's the problem, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: First of all, we don't receive any LiveNote. This is not the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But on page 35, line 4, when mentioning numbers, my colleague mentioned number 1.500 and here it says 15.500. It makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much for that observation. In the meantime, you're not the only ones who are encountering problems with e-court. We, for example, we have it on LiveNote but we cannot make annotations and it's stuck now. It's stuck as well now so. So we are having problems too. Shall we continue or we can only follow on one screen but then if you have documents being shown at the same time, you can only see one screen at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we won't be able to follow the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So the Court and everyone will know, it's just the same numbers basically that we were just discussing. Basically, I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to see them. The accused need to see them. And if it's a document that needs some annotation on our part, unfortunately we are not in a position to do it. At least today. We can do it from our Chambers later, but we do have problems at the moment, technical problems. So we will only proceed if there is unanimous okay on your part. Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Defence teams, is there any Defence team that would like to stop for the time being until this -- no, all right. So we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you have 65 ter number 2D0003 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just quickly describe for us what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a memo from the United Nations protection force in Zagreb addressed to Kofi Annan at the United Nations headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But it has a time and date stamp on the center, right side of that first page, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, dated 19 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the time being 1417, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the subject matter of the memo is "Disposition of Displaced Persons from Srebrenica"; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just quickly to go through this document. I'm sure you'll have time to look at it again. On paragraph number 2 is -- actually I'm telling you this, you can verify it -- is where I obtained the numbers that we were just discussing and it says here, "The joint crisis action team, JCAT", and then it goes on to say where these people were, 6.600 in Tuzla air base. And then it says, "The BiH local authorities report that 18.333 DP", which they reference here, displaced persons, "are accommodated in collection centres with the distribution as follows", then they break them down as I have. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please slow down when he reads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic. Sorry to butt in, but I have a complaint from the interpreters that you're reading too fast. Probably I'm speaking too fast too. And they need some -- a little bit more cooperation on our part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just one of the problems, obviously, it's my fault, primarily, but the secondary, I can't follow it on the screen because of the issue with the screen, so I apologise again to them and to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I asked the question. Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sorry. I was elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand you were reading the document which is interesting. The question basically is where would we find the information as to the makeup of this population of 24.933; how many men, how many women, et cetera? You didn't do the investigation. That was clear to me. Who would have that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian government, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When did you ask them for that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not specifically asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So never, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's okay. Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the reason that the only count that counts for this investigation is a count of people who first went through a detention process so that it doesn't matter any longer if these men were soldiers or civilians, and who later were assassinated. In order to find that number, the only valid process was to identify the location of their burial and go through the entire, and I say, insist on the word entire, exhumation process added to a body count. This is the figure that we were looking for. We were not specifically looking for the figure of men that slipped among the crowd of refugees and arrived safely in the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect, Mr. Ruez, you don't know about this slipping of this one male civilian into this civilian population, right? You're just kind of speculating about that? You don't know because you've never done an investigation to know if that 24.933 population includes 10 per cent or 50 per cent being male, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a compound and getting argumentative. Very difficult to answer a compound question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you rephrase your question, Mr. Ostojic, and split it in various parts. One following the other, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect, Mr. Ruez, you talked about this male slipping in. There is no evidence of that, is there? You're just speculating about that, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring specifically to one witness who is not on the list we have because he's not requested to testify for this trial, but slipping through it is an expression that he used. He managed to cross Kladanj because he knew one of the soldiers on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But did you go and investigate to determine how many or what per cent of that 24.933 were male?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you or do you know if the BiH local authorities maintain still these records as to these individuals who left or as they say here evacuated Srebrenica, Potocari and went to Tuzla? Do you know if those records still exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you think that it's relevant to know what that mix -- make of that population was if the Prosecutor, with whom you worked since 1996, is advocating a position that there was a separation of men and women? Do you think that might be somewhat relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The knowledge we have about the separation process is coming from people who lived through it, as well as the count of more or less everyone who was evacuated from the area and witnessed this separation process. This includes as well the UN military personnel present in Potocari. So this is something that we know as a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll have to study that answer but we will get back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your question was equally not that clear, looking at it again, because I thought for a moment he was not answering the question. And I was going to call on him to try and answer the question. But having looked at your question again, it is not a natural sequence to the previous question and it begs --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it relevant, Mr. Ruez? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was willing to add indeed the thing, to be 100 per cent honest, yes, it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I appreciate that. And it's relevant because if we are going to go to court, we want to give the Court, as we discussed yesterday, a full picture and ultimately a picture of the truth, truly what happened in that situation, correct? That's one of the reasons it's relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I totally agree with that. I'm among the first ones who would expect more truth to come out of these trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's turn to the military column that was going towards Tuzla, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we turn to that topic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So I don't need that exhibit any more. Thank you for the time being, but I will refer to it hopefully later. Now, who gave the estimate as to how many men were in this military convoy from Susnjari going towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The description we have of the situation is not a military convoy. It's a column of people who are fleeing the area and who are mixed with indeed armed military personnel. The estimate is the same thing coming from various sources including the witnesses. And I think it is on this aspect, not on the previous one, that we have an estimate of the intelligence of the Drina Corps, that, I think, provides as well this estimate of 15.000 people somewhere in the woods. So it's a bit of a same situation than previously. It's a rough figure coming from various sources but nothing scientific in it indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise for saying convoy. I didn't mean to misstate it. Column. I was still on the last questions before, so I sincerely meant to say column and not convoy, not to throw you off. What is the margin of error of this estimate, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not dare guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you go and try to confirm from other sources other than the Drina Corps to determine what the amount of people were in this military column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for sure. Again, as I say, all the witnesses who were part of the column gave an assessment of how large they believed it was. The BiH army also had its own assessment. The representatives of the population had their assessment. I mean, all the figures that were coming up were roughly turning around 15.000 and this is why this is the figure commonly used when talking about the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During your investigation, did you come across any sentiment or documents which would state something to the following: Due to the imprecise nature of these figures, we recommend that any public statements are limited to the broad reference of several thousand missing. Did you ever come across that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You as a prudent investigator certainly would have seen that if it exists, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly not. I don't know about every single document talking about this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's flesh out first this military column that we are discussing. Your testimony in other cases, Blagojevic, page 376, line 2, and Blagojevic, page 393, page -- page 393, lines 24 through 27, it's a fact based on your investigation that there were 5.000 armed men in this military column, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was also a figure that was, let's say, a basic figure coming from these various sources. I would now change that, since I don't remember when exactly, but the figure coming from 2nd Corps was that 6.000 men from the 28th division reached the area of Tuzla. So since these are military, I think the figure of 5.000 should be increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you interview or did you know the composition of this military column what division or brigade or battalion they were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all were from the 28th division, and as far as we know, the large amount, the biggest amount of forces was at the top, and at the spearhead of the column, a few troops -- troops mixed among the column and very small force at the end of the column to close the march.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 28th division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not part of the investigation, as you know, but everyone knows that the commander is Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I want to know, and it could be possibly my fault, your investigation was then not limited to a time period, it was limited to investigating crimes purportedly committed by a specific group in the -- at that time, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said it several times. The investigation was about the crimes committed by the Bosnian Serb army or others after the fall of the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying it. Now, during the route of the military column, if you could help me and show me the route that the military column took to try to reach Nezuk. And I think you could use probably page 1 of your exhibit P02103, if we may, on the ELMO. By all means, Mr. Ruez, if you think there is a more appropriate map, then just share that with us and we'll use that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The map you should use is the map of the debriefing of the operation that was conducted by the Drina Corps officers at the Zvornik Brigade, since during the search of the Zvornik Brigade was seized a very large military map on which all elements related to the takeover of the enclave and the fight against the column is on the map. So that would be the most accurate product about this exodus from the enclave, and we had the privilege to have a very detailed expos‚ of that situation by Major Obrenovic during his interview in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's, though -- and we will get to him in a little bit I hope. Let's just use that first exhibit since you looked at it and it was a detailed rendition of the facts. Show me on the first page what the route was, if the Court permits, with a pen or pencil. And I think if you do it on the plastic cover sheet of this document, we will be able to follow it or perhaps even on the e-court system in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: M'hm, we'll put it under the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It cannot be done on e-court. That's for sure. Because they are not in e-court as yet. That's what I am told. Is that correct? So how are we seeing them if they are not in e-court? I see. All right. Okay. All right. So best way of doing it -- is there a hard copy of this that we can place on the ELMO and he can put the markings on it? Whether we have a spare copy to give to the witness, which will be marked -- no, we will need to take it after that. If it is marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Ruez -- the one Mr. Ruez has is probably a good one to use.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel's mike is not on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I want to preserve the integrity of my exhibit book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ruez, Madam Usher, if you could kindly help Mr. Ruez by placing it on the ELMO and we can follow you from there. And, Mr. Ostojic, your microphone is still off. You need to switch it on. And you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The question was pending but I'll repeat it. Sir can you draw on this exhibit, page 1, map, the route of the military column from Susnjari to Tuzla or towards Tuzla as we say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we have it -- could we have a better focussing because it's really --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have to start from the south to the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to move it further up. Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before doing it, I would like to insist on something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do it according to the knowledge that I gained from Major Obrenovic during his interview, though his interview was absolutely not on the topic to get a military teaching on what we call the military operation. This military operation was absolutely not under the focus of the investigation. The fate of that column due to the other concerns that we had was totally out of range of the investigation. So we never went into the details of what happened during, I think, the six days during which this column went out of the area. So do you still want me to do the drawing that is on the map at the Zvornik Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this is Susnjari. Then the column exited the mine field that was around the enclave, heading north towards Kravica area, then turning -- those who didn't know the area had a guideline, that is power line that is along the road, but the column was walking behind the hill. They suffered a severe ambush at a place named Kamenica. The 12 in the evening, the spearhead of the column reached the intersection of Konjevic Polje. The area was not sealed by Bosnian Serb forces. They went through. They went along the Cerska valley, turned around Udrc mountain, made at one point a diversion in order to make a fake attack on Zvornik. Meanwhile, the larger group continued north in order to hit the lines at the level of Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if I could ask you to do two things or three things. First of all, if you could -- where you indicated with a circle Kamenica, if you could write it down, and put your initials next to it, please. All right. And where you put an arrow in the direction of Zvornik, if you could indicate diversion? All right. I haven't seen your initials or your signature. And then you are adding a further arrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just to show the area of Nezuk, here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Did you sign the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I didn't put the date. What is the date today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Today is the 15th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, on this map that we are talking about you see the Kamenica -- you call it an ambush. There was a battle actually between the military column and the Serb forces at Kamenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The report -- I heard of this event. I would not call it a battle. It was an ambush spot. The result of it, and this is why the investigation had an interest on this situation, is that this is what caused the next morning, among other things, but that was the main reason, massive surrender in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now you talked about Mr. Obrenovic's interview. Which interview was it, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember precisely the date. I think it was his second interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was it before or after the plea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in the year 2000, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't know if it was before or after the plea, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What plea?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Mr. Obrenovic? No way, no. This was done in 2003, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it was before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes before, much before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now point out if you can to the best of your recollection -- you're not a military expert, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think you mentioned the naming of Mr. Richard Butler who is for the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So that we are clear on that, I'm not asking you militarily, I'm just asking you as an investigator these questions, and I know you're confining your answers to that so I appreciate it. Can you point out to me during this route where there were other battles or ambushes as you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only being concerned in fact by the fate of those who were trapped in the area and then surrendered to the Serb forces, the main situation is that after the 28 division spearhead managed to break the area in the level of Konjevic Polje, the entire location was sealed by military forces that could be seen by the people who were trying to overlook the asphalt road and everyone was trapped in the area in between Konjevic Polje and more or less the area of Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. Can you tell us the date of that exchange or battle or ambush?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ambush occurred in the late afternoon of July 12. It's in the evening of July 12 that the spearhead of a column went through Konjevic Polje. The next morning, the area was sealed off and that is when the massive surrender process started, 13 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where else other than Kamenica do you have information that there was a battle and/or ambush during this route that the military column took from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we talk about the ordeal of the armed column in between Konjevic Polje and Nezuk, I would not be able to give you any details. We heard them from Mr. Obrenovic, but I don't have precise recollection. There were indeed many engagements ongoing during that escape of the armed part of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But in Krstic's trial on page 494 and 495, a couple of years ago you seemed to remember that there were two ambushes and one being exactly on the Udrc mountain, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. I now remember the statements of those who were at this area, and who indeed said they quickly fled because they were under attack of Serb forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And sir, back to Kamenica if we may, did you do any investigation to determine how many people perished in that battle or ambush?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have a figure in mind. The best investigation, if we can say so in this area, was done by a team of Norwegian experts, forensic experts, who during the year 1996 were doing a body collection process in the area of that ambush. We requested the report of their findings so we must have this in evidence, and there is a body count of skeletons that were collected by this Finnish team from Finland.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of the fact that there were four battles during the route of this column going from Potocari to Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You say four. I don't know your source but I accept it as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We will get into that with Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps for the record we can clarify if we are talking Finland or Norway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he corrected himself in the second instance. So I take it, it was a Finnish group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Finnish.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During these or any of these ambushes, those that you know - and obviously if you know you can share that - did the column actually punch through the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They didn't have to bother with that. The 12 in the evening there were little Serb forces in the area of Konjevic Polje, as far as we know, and their main engagements came later, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about in southwest by Zvornik? Did the column punch through the Serb positions there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe there, since -- but again, this is not something that was the topic of the investigation. Nevertheless, we could find out some aspects. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The lines were open because of a Serb prisoner captured by the 28 division and they had access to his Motorola, so to Serb radio channels. And I think they negotiated with Colonel Pandurevic the possibility to go through the lines. I don't remember the precise dates. It might have been the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did in fact this military column manage to capture anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know they captured equipment on their way indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But you don't know about anti-aircraft guns, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since anti-aircraft guns were used on fix position, it is true that people, yes, they might have come across anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you're fleeing why would you carry an anti-aircraft gun with you, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I could explain it but right now I think it's better if I could finish with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you do because there are --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You'll see the point in a minute, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about mortars, did they capture any mortars, sir, military column from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They -- I would think they didn't carry them during this 70 kilometres of mountain trekking, but, yes, I heard about the fact that in the area of Nezuk, the column did capture Serb equipment and carried -- carry it through the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. How about did the military column manage to capture Serb prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they did that in a circumstance where they were police reinforcements called, and these people were put on trenches in the vicinity of Zvornik, and a group of these was captured in the course of the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And to what extent did you investigate that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not under investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now if I can just read from your testimony that you gave on the Krstic trial, and it's hard because there was a question but you had answered at that time a little lengthier than you have. And I appreciate it and I'm sure all of us do. So there was really never a question, you just spoke a little bit and the Honourable Judge Rodrigues interrupted you to slow down, as they have with me, and to go ahead and conclude with your remarks. So if I can just direct my learned colleague on page 494, starting on page 15, through page 495 through page 2. And I'll read it to you and then we can maybe discuss it and compare it with what you just told us. It states as follows: "I was saying the map is not very precise here because the arrow goes straight above Udrc mountain, which is not realistic, since it's a quite high mountain, very difficult terrain in reality. The movement was much less precise than that. They were turning around. Once they arrived in the area here, which is the southwest of Zvornik, ambushes were set to block this column but these ambushes were not successful. In fact, the column punched through these Serb positions, managed to capture equipment, anti-aircraft guns, mortars, and even managed to capture Serb prisoners." You remember giving that testimony in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say something very different during this one, I think, except that recollection in 2000 was better than the one of 2006. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why is that that the recollection is better whether it's closer to the events? Can you explain that to me as an investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no discrepancy between the two things. When I say punching through the lines, you meant in the area of Konjevic Polje. We are now referring to the area of Nezuk. The opening of the lines was not something that lasted more than a few hours, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to debate it with you. I know we talked about Konjevic Polje and punching through and then we, specifically, I thought went to southwest Zvornik. But that's okay, we will look at the record. The fighting that you described that was going on, you consider it to be "heavy" correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Heaviness of fighting is always something relative.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And that's why my next question is what did you mean when you said heavy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As an example, we know that during this operation, the Zvornik Brigade suffered in one event probably more casualties than during more or less the entire war. That's what we were told. But this will end up coming up with figures and for this I will have to insist on the fact that the final figure of this investigation will be about the people who went through a detention process and this number can be known once the full exhumations will be over. So that number will have to be retrieved from the total number of missing and then you will have the count that you are looking for, those that we can then name killed in action.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know how many were killed in that action at the battle around or near Udrc mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Impossible to make the assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, several years ago I thought you made the assessment on Krstic, page 595. You thought it was 600. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well it's page 595, lines 8 through 17. And at that point --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry on what specific event.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The event that we are discussing, Udrc mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I would think you are referring to the number of bodies at Kamenica that were found by the Finnish team, no? Just to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, because it was somewhat unclear but I thought I followed it and I thought we had it, but we'll clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- at Kamenica to me sounds quite a lot but it's --.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Give us your recollection. Do you think at Kamenica it was 600?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not put a figure. I don't remember. But the number 600 sounds familiar to me, but I don't remember in what context.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again I apologise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to leave this unclear or hazy, as it has emerged now. So if you have the extract from the testimony in Krstic, unless it is available on e-court I suggest you read it out, Mr. Ostojic, and let the -- give the witness a better opportunity to know what you're stating and what he is supposed to tell us. You definitely -- you're referring to losses on one side. He is referring to losses on another side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see. Anyway it's not clear. And this is why I wanted to have it cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you heard our President here, and let's clear that up. From your recollection based on your investigation, there were two ambushes or two battles with this military column, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm always referring to the ambush of Kamenica because this is the area of concern, because this is the area from where the people surrendered. So became prisoners. What happened in between Konjevic Polje and Nezuk, I would not be able to tell you how many ambushes or battles occurred during this part because this was not specifically under investigation. Though we know that indeed there were some moments of heavy fighting happening during this way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ostojic, because you seem to have evaded what I tried to ask you to do. Look at page 54, line 7, please. He's answering your question. Your question was that's correct. That's why my next question is what did you mean when you say heavy? And he answered, as an example, we know that during this operation, the Zvornik Brigade suffered in one event, probably more casualties than during more or less the entire war. Then your next question is: Now, do you know how many were killed in that action at the battle around or near Udrc mountain? He says it's impossible to make the assessment. Then you can go to Krstic, you say it's 595, 600. This is why I would like you to read from Krstic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On page 595 of Krstic, starting with line 8, and again there is more to his answer because at that time he was giving it. So I don't want it to be seen as if I'm only picking portions of it. Just to the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
