utterances.text: But we do agree the Zvornik Brigade he was referring to is the Serb Zvornik Brigade because there was no Muslim Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct. But I'll ask this as the Court wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page 8, I mean line 8, page 595, "This area has been processed in 1996 by a team of experts from Finland who were operating in that area in 1996. Totally disconnected from our activities, they were collecting surface remains. But it's important to note that 600 bodies have been collected in that area and these bodies -- these are bodies of victims killed in combat in ambushes, in shelling and possibly also in other circumstances which are impossible to sort out between -- I mean for us at least, between combat and other situations"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So very simple situation. I was not talking about a general figure as you were trying to put it, related to the entire combat activity. I was specifically talking about the ambush of Kamenica and this number of 600 is indeed the figure that was collected and that we got from the report drafted by the Finnish experts. So indeed at the ambush of Kamenica, I described for you the context of it and the reason why we had an interest in this, generated 600 casualties. This is just a basic fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could continue to read. You gave a lot of information on that. There was an exchange on the next page between the Honourable Judge Rodrigues and our learned colleague Mr. Harmon from the Office of the Prosecution. A video was played and then you go on to say at page 597 line 1, "I guess, in this location, the assessment of victims provided by the witnesses is much more than what has been collected. The numbers usually announced in this area are 1.500 to 2.000 victims but there is a natural inflation of the assessment of numbers in these circumstances."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And this inflation is relating to this 600 bodies, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witnesses who experienced that ambush, when they were then running around and jumping above dead bodies made generally an assessment of a thousand to 1.500 victims in that area. But as I said, during that testimony, the natural instinct in such a situation seems to be inflating numbers. This is why the only reliable source for this event is of a figure of the Finnish team that collected surface remains in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about in Udrc mountain? How many perished from either side, if you know, and then break it down for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will never make a breakdown. The area between Cerska and Nezuk is certainly dotted with surface remains, still nowadays. As far as I know, no one is looking for bodies in this area. I know also about an area with surface remains at Potocari -- at still in the area of the enclave. There are -- there is an unknown number of dead bodies in that countryside.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the expression terrain restoration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a word that I would not be able to say in Serbo-Croatian but that means cleaning up the terrain and burying the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who is burying the dead when they do terrain restoration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army does.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And are they burying their own dead or are they burying the dead of the combatants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are burying all battle casualties for sanitary reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And they bury them how, sir, in graves or in individual plots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Generally, they bulldoze them in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They bulldoze them in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now I want to change and go to another issue if I may quickly. We are discussing ID -- if I can discuss with you IDs, military permits and belongings. And again I'm confining it to the military column leaving Susnjari towards Nezuk, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it true, sir -- I thought I heard you say the other day when you were watching the video used the Serbian word "licna karta". You know what that means, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, identity card.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Identity card. You don't speak Serbian or do you do speak B/C/S, forgive me, B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aside from saying "Dobar dan", I don't speak much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to these identification cards, isn't it true that your investigation, or at the least, you, sir, as a team leader have concluded -- let me start the question again. Thank you. Thank you. Sir, with respect to these identification cards, isn't it true that you in your investigation or you as the investigator in charge of this team have concluded "most of the soldiers were getting rid of any element which could identify them as combatants", correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From whom did you learn that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same situation than in many instances. We discussed its general assessment coming from the interviews conducted with all the people who went through these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that these military men or this military column, they were not stripped of their personal identification cards, they in fact are the ones who threw away those belongings in order not to be identified, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a totally correct. This is the reason why we only use figures related to people who went through a detention process, so that it doesn't make any difference between military people or civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn to another issue if I may quickly. Trying to wrap up. Thank you, Your Honour. And that is Naser Oric. You mentioned him as being the commander of the 28th division, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when did you interview him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never interviewed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever meet with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did meet with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with him in a personal capacity or professional capacity as an investigator for the ICTY Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in a professional capacity of investigator for the ICTY Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have the precise date in mind. At the best of my recollection, I think it was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: December maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sometime in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: End of 1999, yes, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Based on this routine or process that you shared with us, did you have notes from the meeting you had with Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever reduce that to a written statement for Mr. Oric to sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not to get a statement from him, it was to collect information. And I think the only record I had of it was a memorandum summarising the information collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And where is that memorandum now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among the internal material that we have in the archives, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would think so too. Did you ever discuss with him how the military column, the route that they took, the number of men that they had, the amount of arms that they may have had, and the number of people who may have perished as a result of battles through the route of the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Towards Nezuk, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because, again, the investigation was not on that topic. And the reason I was willing to have a meeting with him was to discuss other matters than these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, what matters would that have been, other than the actual investigation that you're conducting for the period that seems to be relevant from July 12 through the 18th of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have in mind -- there were three point, as far as I remember, that I wanted to wash away with him. One being the murder of a man by the name Zikic, a murder that occurred in 1992, and I wanted to clarify a few things with him about this. Another point was in connection with a possibility of identification of a person who was in Potocari during these days, and I wanted to make a check about this one. And the third topic I honestly don't remember at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But why didn't you ask him about the facts that we are discussing here, specifically, the civilians in Potocari and how they were brought or evacuated to Tuzla and the various villages we discussed? Why didn't you ask him about whether that military column that left from Susnjari was actually armed or not armed? Who was the leader of that column? How far or how many ambushes they had? Why didn't you ask him that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For several reasons, but the main reason would be that he would certainly not be the good person to provide information on these aspects, since it's a well known fact that he was not in the area at the time of the events. So he would have nothing relevant except hearsay to testify about in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what, hearsay is not reliable in your opinion? Is that what you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hearsay needs additional investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree. Did you investigate with Mr. Oric whether or not any of his relatives were survivors of any of the massacres that we discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of the points in connection with this investigation was discussed with Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Being a reasonably prudent investigator, if I had a survivor from Orahovac, for example, and if he had the same last name, wouldn't you at least asked Mr. Naser Oric if it's a relative and then verify the circumstances of what you claim that individual may or may not attest to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Family links are irrelevant to me. I knew about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why are they irrelevant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because had Mevludin been identified as a member of Naser Oric's family, he would never have been in this courtroom to testify about what happened to him. So it's not part of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, with all -- just so we can be cautious. I know you testified live but we kept referring to the cheat sheet and I just want to make sure it's okay to mention him by his first name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've been checking precisely that. It's no problem. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking if you asked Mr. Naser Oric if he was related to Mevludin Oric. I'm asking you if you asked him whether or not any of the facts that Mevludin Oric told you on three separate occasions, whether or not that was accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of knowledge about the specific situation Mevludin was into would be -- I don't know what would have to be asked to Naser about what happened to his cousin. I mean it's -- doesn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: In 2003, isn't it correct that it was your opinion -- another topic, sorry -- with respect to exhumations, you said "We are now in 2003, eight years after the events. We have located probably 95 per cent of all these graves." Do you remember giving that statement in the Blagojevic case, page 729, line 9 through 12, sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now we are even more removed, three years or more, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What per cent does it increase or decrease that I can use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only one site has been found since year 1993. It is a site located in Potocari that was discovered by the team of Mr. Masovic. This is so maybe we are now at 96 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's your estimate, 96 per cent, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's impossible to make an estimate since we might never find absolutely all the graves related to this operation, but this is more or less my belief, in terms of global results of this identification process of mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Just so it's clear in the record, on page 64, line 18, you start your answer by saying only one site has been found since the year 1993, but you really mean since the year 2003 since that's what we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, not 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's okay. Just for the record. I understood you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I often mix the years ninety and 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir did you ever ask Mr. Oric how many of the military -- how many -- in this military convoy, how many military men came to Tuzla ultimately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because again he was not the, let's call it, the man in charge at that time. I got the figure by 2nd Corps command and I told you that figure was 6.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who was that from? Where did you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first source was AID, and then that was the figure that came up during informal conversations both with Major Tihic who became Colonel Tihic and also the deputy of the 2nd Corps, I don't remember his name. We interviewed him I would think in 1999 and he gave that figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now you mentioned earlier that AID is a form of secret service, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the so-called.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For who, though?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the people in Bosnia, that's how I name this service.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs, the Bosnian Croats or the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You would think for everyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's state security, so people call it secret service.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. So Mr. Bourgon or Madam Nikolic, I don't know who is going. Break will be in another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry. If I can interrupt my learned colleague. I did want to ask one last question with the Court's permission. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, I noticed a blue pin on your jacket. What is that just out of curiosity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is an insignia of the national order of merit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I understand that the witness will be answering my questions in English but I will be asking my questions in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is free to answer you in French if he so chooses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I only have a few questions to ask. While I thought -- I only have a few questions for you. Yes. We may resume. Good morning, Mr. Ruez. I only have a few questions to ask you this morning, after the questions asked by my colleague. You confirm that you were the chief investigator in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. [In English] About the fact that though Mr. Bourgon is a French speaker and so am I, I continue to testify in English because I prefer to be accountable for my own words in the common working language of this Court rather than taking the risk of being cross-examined in a few years with potential translation misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. That may also apply to you, later on. You may be faced with having put one question when you actually meant to put another. But any way, go ahead, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Being French Canadian, I don't think I should ask my questions in English from a French-speaking witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you are the chief investigator in this -- besides the statement concerning the interceptions which was discussed with my colleague a bit earlier yesterday, you didn't give any statement concerning your work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't produce any final report for this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The investigator Alistair Graham was an investigator who worked with you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was an investigator in the team. Then he left the team to serve as head of office in Pristina, Kosovo, and when I left the Tribunal, it was of a common agreement with everyone that he would take the lead after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Ruez, is rather specific. This gentleman worked with you and I would like to know Mr. Graham will be a witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea if Mr. Graham will be a witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why are you asking Mr. Ruez? You ask Mr. McCloskey that question. I mean he's not the one who is going to decide. It's true that he told us -- he made statements to effect that he knew of some persons who were going to be witnesses in this case but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not trying to establish whether Mr. Graham will in fact testify or not. I know that. I'm simply trying to establish whether the witness knows and then I will ask the witness whether the reason why he never asked his investigator to produce a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is the purpose of my questioning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Mr. Ruez, my question is rather simple. I just wish to know whether it is true that you have never asked Mr. Graham to compile a statement as an investigator for this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say that your question is vague to me because asking him to compile a global report on this investigation, I would never had been able to ask him such a thing because meanwhile I was the team leader. That would have been my responsibility to do so, and in terms of asking him declaration about something else, I would need to know what that would have been about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you know the difference between an investigation report and the fact of giving a statement which can be given to the Defence for the case you know the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- because the system is not in use in France. In France we produce a final investigation report that we address either to the prosecutor or to the investigative judge. We do not prepare -- the entire file is provided to the defence. So I'm not familiar with declaration to be given to the defence or I forgot about it since I've left this place now since a couple of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Therefore, I'll go directly. Do you know the investigator, you know he did not make a statement concerning his work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have met Tomasz before starting to testify in this court. It was the first time I met him. I'm sure he arrived in this place a long time after I had left it, so I have no idea about whatever statement he was supposed to do or not do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript, Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Ruez, does not mention the name of this person you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be edited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm just pointing it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President. Mr. President, the name I've mentioned, just to be precise, is Tomasz Blaszczyk, although I don't know exactly how to pronounce this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ruez, what about Brett Randall, did he work with you? Do you know whether he has given or no statement concerning his work in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Brett Randall, he stayed a very, very short time within the team. And there was designed to join another one fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ruez, what about Eileen Gilleece, also an investigator? Did she also make a statement towards being a witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat that name?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. Eileen Gilleece.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear about this name for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Ruez, when the facts which have to do with your testimony in this case have been heard for the first time in the framework of Krstic case, you were at the time the chief investigator. I would like to know why no investigator for this file, for those who were witnesses in that case, you didn't think it was a right thing to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I do not see really the point in respect of this declaration. The useful documents, as far as I know, are either produced by investigators who then become expert witnesses, so that was the case for Dean Manning, as an example. For the rest, due to the adversarial process here, I used to say that the file is in the heads of those who are called to testify, because at no moment was it ever said by the Prosecution here that any type of global report had to be submitted at what point or another before trial. But I say that in France it is indeed the common habit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. What I was trying to establish, there has been no statement made because you believed that it wasn't something that was requested from you, or which was necessary for this case. So we agree on this point, don't we, for this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... initiative to request such a declaration, nor was I, nor was it requested by the Prosecution, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. The few questions I'm asking at this stage are just general questions concerning the methodology used during your -- the investigation. If I understood your testimony up to now, you went for the first time on the site of the incidents on the 20th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Therefore, if I put to you that before the 20th of July 1995, you had no knowledge, no personal knowledge, of what could have happened on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during your investigation, you did actually lead several interviews with possible witnesses, some of which were survivors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In certain cases it was established during the answers you gave to the questions of my colleague, you took statements while in other cases you only took notes or sometimes nothing at all. Isn't it the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That's not the case. For all the witnesses of these events, I mean let's say the group of victims, in a large sense of that word, statements were systematically taken. Only in a very few instances were contacts made without keeping records of it. Most of the time on a, let's say on a conscious base of doing it so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, these interviews, they were also done by investigators working under your orders who themselves had several interviews for which in certain cases we have the statement and in other cases we only have notes. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not so sure. I don't have a precise recollection of the investigators of the team who -- no. There are instances indeed. Most of the time, contacts were finalised through interviews. Only in some specific instances no interview was taken and only either notes or written admin reports about the contact, depending on the specificity of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps we can clarify this a little bit. Within the Office of the Prosecutor, when you had teams going on site to investigate, did you have a protocol? Did you have a set practice that you needed to follow across the whole Office of the Prosecutor or was each investigator or each team leader free to adopt his or her own system of investigation and method of archiving and reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As long as the Rules of Evidence and Proceedings were followed, there was no common practice, indeed. Everyone, as far as I know, because I didn't have time to look into the way other investigations were conducted, but in fact, indeed, everyone was doing according to his experience and background. I can say it's so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have the break now, Mr. Bourgon, or do you wish to proceed for another minute or so?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If that's the pleasure of the Court, we can fold right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ruez, we shall continue on the topic we were talking about before the pause, which is to say the preparation of the investigation. Just to give you an indication I've got six topics which I would like to cover in my cross, and I think we will be able to finish before the end of this hearing and, as much as possible, I will ask you, though it won't always be possible, but as much as possible I would like you to try and answer by yes or no whenever possible. Therefore, we were talking before pause that several interviews had taken place, both with you and the investigators placed under your orders. My question is the following: Now that you are giving this testimony, are you in agreement with me that it's not always easy to remember everything which may have been told to you by all these witnesses before answering a question which is being asked from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during your testimony, at our request, or at the request of Defence counsel, you were asked to specify your sources, sources on which your testimony was based. Would you agree with me that the sources you mentioned during your testimony are not necessarily all the sources which may have given you some information concerning the questions which were asked from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Among the sources you mentioned answering our questions, some to your knowledge will be witnesses while others will not be witnesses in this trial. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I did understand the nature of your testimony to this Chamber since the beginning of the week, I put to you that your goal, obviously if I understood you, was to describe and to give an overview view, a general overview to the Chamber of what the witnesses called by the Prosecution will come and say. Is this true and correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that is correct indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, during your investigation, you met and you have used the services of several specialists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the other hand, you yourself are neither an anthropologist, nor an archeologist nor a pathologists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You are neither an expert in ballistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not an expert in ballistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Therefore, when you recorded what was said by these specialists, your goal was to give an overview of what they will come and say to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I mentioned elements they will testify about and develop, yes, indeed, that was the objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, specifically on the question of expertise in ballistics, could you confirm that you have indeed proceeded with expertise with specialists and that your goal was to establish links between primary and secondary graves but the results were not reliable and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No this is not the case. Yes, indeed, we proceeded with experts to the analysis of the shell casings collected both on the surface of the execution sites to be compared with those shell casings found inside the primary mass graves and to be later on compared with those found inside the secondary mass graves, and I have to totally disagree with you when you say that the results were not reliable or that this process was of no interest. It's exactly the opposite, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that the procedure is without interest. My question was much more specific. I put to you that these expertise in ballistics did not enable you to put a link between a primary and secondary mass graves, as you call them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the point on which I say that you have a totally reversed your statement. These ballistics expertise have produced results and links between the sites, as it was explained in detail by expert Dean Manning, who was an investigator in the team and who will come again for this trial to present the evidence to the Court, as far as I know, or maybe you have the report that he provided for the sake of the Krstic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ruez, if I put to you, if I mentioned that both in the Blagojevic trial where you were a witness, as well as in the Krstic trial, where you also were a witness - I don't have the precise source now with me but I'll find it - you mention then the fact that the ballistic experts, the fact of having shot several shots with weapons you had, the results were not conclusive. Do you remember having said that during your testimonies, both in the Blagojevic and in the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I want to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a misstatement and a miss mischaracterisation of those trials but perhaps it can be cleared up by answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been better, Mr. Bourgon, that when you stated this you would have started mentioning that indeed I was referring to a totally different operation than the shell casing comparison from what I said the execution sites. The primary mass graves and the secondary mass graves, that was not what you were talking about. You are talking about a series of searches that we conducted in order to seize and test fire some 3.000 weapons that we believed were at that time in possession of the brigades we suspected of participation in the crimes committed, and though we tried that operation, we also knew that 15.000 of the weapons available in the area had been refurbished and that there had been movements of weapons between the brigades. We still did that operation, and, indeed, the result of this massive effort ended up totally unconclusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez, but this was not the point in my question. I'll come back to it when I've found my sources but I will have later on questions to ask you precisely on this topic of these weapons found in the sector. Now, about your investigation, I have a last question to ask of you. During your testimony you said that when you arrived in Tuzla for the first time, you had spoken to three different sources and you said one of them of these three sources was the AID, or the secret services rather. Personally, I'm surprised to see for what reason you went to this secret services in order to obtain statements? And I put to you that rather it is the secret services, AID, who contacted you and not the reverse. Could you please specify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. AID was a contact point for the Office of the Prosecutor, and the contact with AID was organised through a person who is a member of the OTP and who was constantly on the ground in Sarajevo, though at that time there was no Sarajevo office in place. His name is Matthew Hudus [phoen], an American citizen. So it's a bit like the chicken and the egg in that matter. I don't know if indeed we approached them. I know I did. But indeed the contact was pre-established between the Bosniak authorities and the Tribunal, and one of these channel of contacts was AID.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Allow me, Mr. Ruez, to specify my question. Why approach the secret services information or intelligence sources to obtain statements from the people who arrived in Tuzla? This is the link I'm trying to establish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason is simple. We had the knowledge that once the refugees arrived in Tuzla, AID, that is also a part of the police, though the appellation, secret service, started the process of interviewing as much people as possible and they did that, I think, during at least two or three weeks, so they already had what I called a reservoir of available statements, though the statements that were taken by them were very rough statements, half a page, one-page statement per person. But it was a good starting base for us in order to scan potential witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. I don't doubt that these statements could be useful for your inquiry, for your investigation, but we can confirm that your investigation allowed to confirm that the refugees as soon as they had arrived in Tuzla got interviewed by secret services of Bosnia. That is indeed the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to correct it slightly. We already gave a figure of these refugees, 25.000. So, no, not all the refugees were interviewed by the Tuzla police, though among them AID people, but those who had relevant information or believed having relevant information were invited to give a statement. I have to add that it's not because they were interviewed by AID that we considered them as being either of a high value, either of no value, because being at a first stage interviewed by AID. We made our own assessment of that information after we proceeded to the interview ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. What I would like to avoid is to -- having to interrupt you. The point of my question were the refugees, when they arrived in Tuzla, yes or no, were interviewed by the secret services. At the time you confirmed that it was indeed the case, it's the only point I was getting to with my question. Isn't it the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the reason why I wanted to make it more precise. No, the refugees were not interviewed because they were 25.000. A few hundred of them have been indeed interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is the answer. This is the question I hope you would answer. Now, I go to another topic, the question of the column, the people who, according to your testimony and the answers which you gave to my colleague, would have left through the woods to go to Tuzla. Answering questions of my colleague, you mentioned, and you also said in the Blagojevic trial, there was, according to you, about 15.000 men in this column, indeed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the Blagojevic trial, during your testimony you separated this column in two groups. On the one side the army and the unarmed men on the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I would hike you to confirm is your assumption, you mentioned this during your testimony in the Blagojevic trial, and I am precisely going to use the words you spoke in the Blagojevic, page 393, lines 22 to 24. In that trial, you said, and I'm quoting you, "[In English] As I indicated previously, the number of soldiers of the 28th division was determined by the number of weapons available." [Interpretation] Is this indeed the assumption you used during your investigation, which is to say that the number of soldiers which were identified was determined using the number of weapons which were available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I meant with that is that -- and I'm sure the Defence will not contradict me on that point -- the situation within the enclave, in terms of combat force, would not only be the combat force of members who would have military card saying they are members of the 28th division, but the fact that every man of military age, if he had access to a weapon, could be indeed considered as an additional fighting force available. Also, I think we have a document in the records, there was a mobilisation order coming from the local authorities in Srebrenica that came out a few days before the fall of the enclave. So that means again that any man, let's say, wearing either a shirt or a camouflage uniform, could be legitimately considered as a combatant. Nevertheless, I always insist on one thing. This investigation only deals with people who first went through a detention process before being assassinated. This is why there is absolutely no problem for the Prosecution side to characterise every single male of fighting age in the enclave as a potential threat for the Serb [Realtime transcript read in error "reserve"] forces, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. I wasn't asking for so much but I'm happy with your answer since it corresponds to what you said during your testimony in two previous trials. I shall now shift to another topic, or rather a last question about the beginning of the events, that is to say in the Blagojevic trial, you said that there was a number of unknown men who went to Potocari because they didn't want to abandon their families. Is this a fact which was established during your investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Just before answering, I noticed a mistake in the transcript. I didn't say reserve forces but Serb forces, if you pointed it out as well. I don't have the line under the eyes. But to return to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's page 80, line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To return to your question, yes, indeed, this is what we learned from people that we had interviewed and who went through the Potocari events. There were various reasons given about the motivation --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to interrupt you, Mr. Ruez. The question was limited to confirming that your investigation has established that there were a number of men who went to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You agree. And further to the questions asked by my colleague a bit earlier, you can confirm that you do not know how many these men were, what the number of these men were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, as we have seen in a video, which you showed during your testimony, you can confirm that among these men some were in military age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'll now move no a site called Grbavci. I'd like to confirm that according to your investigation the school of Grbavci was identified as being a detention place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. One answer is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic, one answer is not. Yes, exactly. The reason is that we are moving too fast, even though counsel and witness are not speaking the same language. Could I ask you again to repeat your question, please? And then he will -- the question I can read it out myself. We have seen in a video, Mr. Ruez, which you showed during your examination-in-chief, can you confirm that amongst these men, some were in or of military age? And then I heard your answer but it doesn't show up in the transcript. Could you kindly repeat your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yes. It was confirmed that the Grbavci school was indeed identified as a detention place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are on different wave lengths.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can take from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes of course by all means. It's the previous question that you don't -- according to the transcript you don't seem to have answered but in actual fact you had answered it and I heard you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez the question, if you can find the line, your answer should appear at page 82, line 1, where it says that your microphone wasn't switched on. So I'll resume this question. Among the people, the men, who decided to go to Potocari, you may confirm according to the elements you got into your investigations that some of them, there are going to be specific, both had the -- well in military age and were in a state to fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let us come back to the Grbavci school. According to your investigation, you can confirm that the sites you have named, LZ 1 and LZ 2 would have been primary mass graves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't use the word alleged. I said they were primary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Alleged comes from my side, but this has not been established. The Tribunal couldn't establish this from their side. Now, according to what one could read in your previous testimony, in the Blagojevic case, the first checks made concerning the size of Grbavci were done in April 1996, that is to say a year after the events of July 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Precisely nine months after, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And still, according to your testimony in the Blagojevic trial, can you confirm that you went back on site on the ground several times indeed but, more specifically, in 1999 with so-called survivors -- I say so-called; that's the way you called them. So, the goal being to ask them to identify the site of executions which they were not able to do, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This I will not answer yes or no. I will explain you the process of that. First I returned but for other purposes --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, just allow me. I just want to spare time. I don't want to interrupt you but I just want to quote what you said in the Blagojevic trial, page 489, line 16 to 21, in order to be able to -- because I see we only have 15 minutes left and I would like to make some head way. Blagojevic trial page 489, line 16 to 21. [In English] "After we went there, we presented first photographs to the victims but in 1999, we brought the victims back to these, to these sites, and indeed they recognised that school as being the one. But we did not enter the school with the victims. The goal was to bring them, to try to have them bring us, in fact, to the execution sites to check if they were able to find it. But they were not." [Interpretation] Is this testimony which you recognise having made in the Blagojevic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise it but I have to modify it slightly. I said we didn't bring them back inside the school. I was wrong. We did bring them back inside the gym and I remember the fact that they were pointing to us precisely where they were sitting inside the gym and the position in which they were sitting, and I didn't have that in mind when I testified in 2003. For the second part of what I said, it is absolutely true that they were unable to find the location, but there is a very easy explanation about it, but I don't know if you want to hear this explanation but there is a very simple --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No. No. I will save your explanation. Perhaps a colleague can ask the question during his cross but I just want you to confirm that these witnesses were not able to find or identify the site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... someone will pick up the point later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move to another question, Mr. Ruez. During the examination-in-chief, you explained that you found near the Grbavci school a pile of waste that you analysed, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The pile of debris in -- next to the playground of the Grbavci school, if it's the one you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed. In this regard, in the Blagojevic case, you stated that that school the Grbavci school, was also used from time to time by the army and that as a result the items found in that heap, especially the shell casings were not necessarily to be linked with the events of July 1995. Do you remember testifying in this way in the Blagojevic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I absolutely do, and I do make this type of comments in the frame of the fact that I am not biased. Therefore, when there is an information that can exclude responsibility or wrong assumptions I point them out and I did it during that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's very much to your credit, Mr. Ruez. Another fact that you mentioned which is from the same category, during your investigation, you stated that none of the prisoners, people allegedly detained in that Grbavci school, said to you that they would have heard bursts of fire coming from location close by the school. Do you remember saying so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, and we found an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe. Maybe you did. Maybe you have an explanation. But all that interests me right now is whether or not there were prisoners who would have stated something else during your investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like now to deal with a very specific topic regarding LZ 1 and LZ 2. It sort of titillated my curiosity during your testimony. I'm referring to Monday, 11 September, page 14899 of the transcript, line 13 to 15. 1489. Page 85, line 25, your answer was not mentioned in the transcript because your microphone was not activated. So I will an ask you to simply repeat your answer. My question was as follows: During your investigation, when you spoke to people who were detained in the Grbavci school, none of them revealed or said that they had heard bursts of fire close by, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Back to my other question which I'd started, so on Monday the 11th of September you explained a location and described it which, on the basis of the information provided by a survivor, as you said, that would have been a resting area for the members of the execution squad. My question is a simple one: Which survivors are we speaking about? If you need to mention a name specifically we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I raised that point again during this testimony, when I showed the area on the surface of which we found these carton boxes that are used to condition the ammunition rounds. We would have to retake the statements that we have in records for the four survivors in that place. I cannot remember which one of them specifically raised the point about this so-called rest area. I have no recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. As far as I'm concerned, I looked into the entire documents made available to me, what you call survivors whether they are going to be witnesses or not and I did not find a single trace of any allusion being made to the fact that there was a rest area for the so-called members of the execution squad. Could this be that it's just a conclusion you drew upon finding those munition boxes there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't think, but I have to trust you when you say you made the check, so I could not exclude this because indeed the observations made on the ground showed that the area I labelled "rest area" was in no way used to shoot people on that spot, but indeed elements were found showing that this was a location where the soldiers might have used to prepare their business. So I cannot exclude if you say that it might have been a conclusion that I now believe having come from someone. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question regarding the LZ 1 and LZ 2 sites, when you testified in the Blagojevic case, you said, and I'll ask you to confirm this, you said that the total amount of bodies found connected with the Grbavci events, both from primary and secondary sites, would amount to 493 bodies. You said this on page 15499, lines 5 to 7. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not only I confirm but I would have to say that this is not a final number because unfortunately the process of the exhumation of the secondary graves on the Hodzici road is not finalised yet so I would assume that once this exhumation process will be over and the connections made, this number will be above 493 bodies coming from these Orahovac execution sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the time being, this figure of 493 was established during your investigation and you mentioned it in the Blagojevic trial; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move to another location, the Hodzevic [phoen] school. You testified about it and I have a very -- very few brief questions. First of all, during your investigation, prior to 1999, you had no indication that people were detained in that school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think when I said 1999 it's even -- it's not precise because, in fact, though we assumed it was used, the certainty came after my departure from the Tribunal, following an interview that was conducted with one element of a Bosnian Serb army who was guarding the men detained at that school. So in fact, this was confirmed after 2001 but the pictures that I showed were taken far before that date because we had a very strong feeling that school indeed had been in use.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question on this and try to be brief in your answers because we only have a few minutes left. What are your sources providing you with this information in 2001, as you stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got the information from someone who is still in connection with the investigation at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you give us the name of the said individual? Can you confirm whether or not this individual is going to be a witness in our trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is more a question that you should address to the Prosecutor, because I'm not the master of the schedule of intervention of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yeah, but you have the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have the name of the person who was present at the Grbavci school, but the Prosecutor has the name of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll stop there, because I have obtained the element I wanted to ascertain. I'm going to try to finish today so that my colleagues can then start next Monday. One quick question regarding the photographs, the aerial photographs, not to mention the sources thereof just the pictures themselves. In these photographs, you showed that there were buses visible, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's vague. If there -- there is several photographs, different buses, unless it can be general it might be helpful to have a more specific direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed. If you're referring to the Bratunac one, then refer to the Bratunac one but we've seen several photos with what appear to be buses and what he indicated as buses. So -- I don't know what your question is going to be, your next question is going to be so --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My question was very general, precisely so as to avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In some of these photographs can we see buses? And the fact that these buses are visible in these photographs, does it make it possible for you to say whether inside the buses there were women and children on their way to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not also give the colour of the eyes of the driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if you have no further questions, let's stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the witness answered the first part of the question but it's not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It -- basically, what we should have is in line 17, after the first part of that question, some of these photos, can we see buses, he did answer yes. All right, any further questions, Mr. Bourgon? Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just one last question in conclusion and then the floor can be given to my colleagues at the next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On the basis of your investigation, Mr. Ruez, according to what you said it was established that General Mladic was seen speaking to detained people in Bratunac, in the Sandici meadow, in Nova Kasaba and in the Grbavci school, is it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I testified about that during the public hearing of the end of June, early July 1996, where I pinpointed on a map all the locations where General Mladic was identified and seen by witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to show you a video that was used during your examination-in-chief, it's only three seconds. 65 ter 2047. I will only ask you to identify one individual in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When this video recording was shown, you were asked to identify some individuals. Can you identify the man in black who is kissing General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At least not on this specific photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We maybe should show it again just these few seconds to see whether you recognise the man who is kissing General Mladic. Maybe seen from another angle, you will be able to recognise him. Is it possible to show it again very rapidly?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm talking about the man in black, who seems to be quite tall, at least two metres high, dark hair, that man, can you identify him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only see his back and at one point, a short shot of his profile and, no, this face doesn't sound familiar to me and this back doesn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ruez. One very last question for you. As the chief investigator in this case, did you participate in discussions during which the statement of facts jointly filed by the Prosecution and the counsel of Dragan Obrenovic were drafted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment I just want to make sure his answer is shown on the transcript. It's not. Could you repeat your answer, please, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer of what, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The answer to his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is no, I did not participate in these conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask of the remaining Defence teams how much time you require. Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A certain part of our cross-examination will not be for Monday but in total maybe one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One hour. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between one hour and one hour and a half, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic? Half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, very little. I may not even have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Same answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you should be able to come on Monday and go back to beautiful Paris. I heard from my daughter that the weather is not good today over there so ... Yes, Mr. Bourgon, my attention is being drawn to the fact that you did not mention the 65 ter number of the video that the witness was shown. That you would like to do so? I should say it in French, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did mention the number. I did mention the number, 65 ter 2047.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I did mention the number, Mr. President. I would never forget that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It didn't go into the transcript. So that's it. A word of thanks to the staff, the interpreters, and the technicians, everyone present, for having stayed with us for a further seven minutes and I wish everyone a happy weekend. To you as well, Mr. Ruez, and thank you for staying with us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
